title: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
summary: Pope Leo XIV's historic France visit includes a private meeting with abuse victims in Lourdes and a Saturday Mass expecting up to 1 million people.
story: Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday, Sept. 25, starting a four-day tour across Paris, Lourdes, and Metz that includes speeches and a massive outdoor mass. (HOST BROADCASTER via Reuters.)

Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.

French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.

"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

The pope will visit Metz on Sept. 28, 2026 to conclude his four-day state and pastoral trip to France, which also includes stops in Paris and Lourdes. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images)

The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."
In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS

The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants, the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.
President of France Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron welcome Pope Leo XIV to Élysée Palace on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France.  (Tom Nicholson/Getty Images)

French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.

Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II, on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.
Pope Leo XIV attends the Welcome Ceremony at Paris Orly International Airport on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France.  (Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)

Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right.
POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS

On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."

The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.

A crucifix stands in front of the Basilique Notre-Dame du Rosaire, its spire draped with a banner marking the upcoming visit of Pope Leo XIV, five days ahead of the pontiff's trip to the site as part of his apostolic journey to France, in Lourdes on Sept. 22, 2026.

Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.

He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend.
Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: ‘It was a mess’: Tennessee fails to execute inmate after 2 lethal injections
summary: Christa Pike, 50, was an accomplice in a murder she committed at 18. She would be the first woman executed by the state in more than 200 years.
story: Tennessee failed to execute the lone woman on its death row as planned Wednesday, even after injecting her with a lethal drug, a stunning development after the Supreme Court had stepped in to allow the state to put her to death.

Attorneys for Christa Pike said Wednesday night that she was being treated at a hospital, but they did not know her condition. A spokesperson for the Department of Correction did not answer an emailed question whether she was alive but said she was “transported to an off-site medical facility.”
Pike, 50, is the state’s only woman on death row. She was convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995, when she was 18 years old, and sentenced to death.

In a news conference Wednesday night, journalists who witnessed the attempted execution described snoring and complaints from Pike about pain, as well as her kicking her feet so often that she knocked off the sheets laid on her. At times, the curtain was closed and journalists could only hear sounds.
In a federal court filing seeking to halt her execution, Pike’s lawyers said witnesses saw executioners injecting “both syringes of lethal injection chemicals” but that Pike remained alive.
They said Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat” and that curtains to the death chamber “have gone down twice,” according to the lawyers.

Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, said in a statement that he was ordering “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” He added that the last remaining execution for this year will not be carried out as planned.
In a phone interview with NBC News early Thursday morning, May Martinez, the mother of victim Colleen Slemmer, described the execution attempt.
“It was a mess,” she said.
‘Nothing about today was normal’
An ambulance was seen arriving at the prison where Pike was to be executed and then leaving. Medical aid was being administered, according to online federal court records.

“It appeared that this did not go like they thought it was supposed to go,” said John North, investigative producer at WBIR television in Knoxville. “But we don’t know that. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”
Tori Gessner, a reporter and anchor at WKRN of Nashville who has witnessed five executions in the state, said at a news conference that, “Nothing about today was normal, typical, at all.”
Gessner said that at 7:34 p.m. Pike was heard saying, “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open.” Pike then talked about that spot on her arm and asked, “Does this happen like that?” Gessner said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Correction said the state “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office” and that “the lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective.”

It’s the second time an execution did not go as planned in Tennessee this year. Tony Carruthers, convicted in three 1994 killings, was granted a one-year reprieve after executioners in May couldn’t find a vein for a backup IV.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement.
The execution warrant for Pike was set to expire at midnight local time (1 a.m. ET Thursday). The Department of Correction did not immediately say if they would attempt another execution, or when.
The process to execute Pike began at about 8 p.m., her lawyers said, after the Supreme Court vacated a lower court’s Wednesday morning order that had temporarily blocked the move.

The high court’s decision hours later capped a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering in a bid by Pike’s defense team to spare her life. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
Victim’s mother furious

“They went to try to execute her, and she didn’t die,” said Martinez, who wanted the execution carried out and was furious with the state’s governor, the director of the Department of Correction and the attorney general.
Martinez said Pike never expressed remorse during Wednesday’s attempted execution. “Not nothing. That sorry about what happened, you know, to Colleen,” Martinez said.
She criticized the communication about what was going in from officials.
“They didn’t say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. And we left,” Martinez said.
“We didn’t know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner,” Martinez said. “And he said that it didn’t work, that it didn’t work, and she’s on her way to the hospital.”
Asked what her message to the governor and attorney general was, Martinez was terse in her response: “They f----- up.”
Appeals court stayed execution, based on child abuse claims

About an hour before her scheduled execution at 10 a.m. local time in Nashville, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said it needed to review claims made by her lawyers. At issue was whether Pike could reopen a court proceeding centered around her allegations that she was sexually abused beginning when she was a child — abuse that the state did not dispute at a special hearing in August.
The appeals court in a split decision agreed to a “short” reprieve halting her execution “in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”
In turn, the state attorney general’s office asked the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that the execution needed to go on to “avoid rewarding Pike’s abusive delay tactics.”

In their dissent, the three liberal justices wrote that vacating the lower court’s temporary stay of execution “interferes with the Sixth Circuit’s routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim.”
“I see no reason to shortcircuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Sotomayor wrote.
Lee and the Supreme Court had said this week they would not stop Pike’s execution.
Before she learned Monday that Lee would not intervene in her case, Pike wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser: “Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace.”
“I am not afraid to die,” wrote Pike, who has been on death row for more than three decades. “I’m only nervous about the process.”
Pike was set to be the first woman in more than 200 years that the state has put to death, according to historical records.

In 1995, Knoxville police said, she and two teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Slemmer, 19. Police said Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.

The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”

title: California voters back a billionaire tax, but the proposal falls short of majority support
summary: A new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group shows “yes” supporters leading 48% to 38% on the California ballot measure.
story: A plurality of likely California voters support a proposal on the state’s November ballot that would impose a one-time wealth tax on the richest Californians, but the measure is still short of majority support, according to a new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group poll released Wednesday.
In the poll, 48% said they would vote “yes” on the proposal, while 38% said they would vote “no.” Another 14% said they were undecided.
The 10-point lead for “yes” is outside the poll’s margin of error, which is plus or minus 4 percentage points for each side’s support level.

The spread was almost identical among Hispanic likely voters, according to a companion survey of California: 50% said they’d vote “yes,” 40% said they’d vote “no,” and 10% said they were undecided. Both surveys were conducted Sept. 21-24.

The so-called billionaire tax — which will appear on the November ballot as “Proposition 40” — would implement a one-time 5% tax on the assets of Californians with net worths exceeding $1.1 billion, and it would require the state to spend 90% of the new revenue on healthcare. The remaining 10% would be split between education and food assistance programs.

In addition to the one-time tax on those worth more than $1.1 billion, the measure, if it is passed, would implement a smaller tax on individuals worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

The ballot measure comes amid a growing wealth gap nationwide — and growing ill feeling toward the ultra-wealthy, driving populist campaigning in the 2026 midterm elections. In an earlier national NBC News poll, raising taxes on billionaires was the most popular candidate attribute out of 15 tested.

Meanwhile, progressive candidates proposing higher taxes on billionaires have seen success in numerous elections throughout the country, although not all efforts to raise taxes on the wealthy have gone smoothly. In New York City, a judge has pressed pause on Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s bid to tax valuable second homes, citing issues with how Mamdani’s administration implemented the plan.

In California, the billionaire tax proposal on the ballot has divided Democratic leaders. Prominent proponents — including Rep. Ro Khanna, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Tom Steyer, a billionaire activist who unsuccessfully ran for governor — argue it would help close income inequality gaps and help make up for state budget shortfalls as a result of Medicaid cuts in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”

Opponents of the ballot measure, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic candidate to succeed him this year, Xavier Becerra, have argued the initiative would drive wealthy investors and tech leaders from the state.

The details of the proposal, which has been led by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, a large California healthcare workers union, have also sparked opposition from many other unions and Democratic groups. Those groups have taken issue with the fact that other progressive policy priorities, like public education and food assistance, would benefit far less than healthcare from the new revenue.

Many Democratic critics have also joined forces with some Republicans, many of whom have long argued that a wealth tax could destabilize California’s revenue streams by causing the ultrarich to flee the state.
But the new poll showed California voters were largely not worried about the prospect of wealthy California residents’ leaving.

A total of 59% of respondents said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned about that potential outcome, while a total of 41% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about rich people’s leaving the state because of the ballot measure. Among Hispanic voters, 62% said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned, while 38% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned.
For Subscribers
Notably, the poll also found California voters almost evenly split over whether they approve or disapprove of the job performance of Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful.
For Subscribers

Forty-five percent of respondents said they approved of his job performance, while 46% said they disapproved. Another 9% said they weren’t sure. Hispanic voters were more positive about Newsom, with 54% approving and 38% disapproving of his performance as governor.

But when it came to how Democrats felt about a possible Newsom 2028 bid, they overwhelmingly said they’d get behind him. Asked whether they’d be inclined to vote for him if he ran to become the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee in 2028, 66% of Democratic respondents said yes, 15% said no, and 19% said they weren’t sure.

Another November ballot measure, Proposition 39, would, if it is passed, require voters to show a government-issued ID when they cast ballots in person, while mail-in voters would have to provide the last four digits of a designated ID used during registration. Among likely voters, 49% said they would support the measure, while 42% said they would vote against it, and 9% said they were undecided.
Asked about Proposition 39, 55% of Hispanic voters said they would vote “yes” in support of it, while 38% said they would vote “no,” and 7% said they were undecided.

California voters strongly said cost of living and the economy were among the most important issues when they were deciding to vote, with 25% saying “cost of living/inflation” was the most important and 23% saying “economy/jobs.” Another 15% said “immigration and enforcement” was the most important, while 11% said healthcare, and 10% said “foreign policy and the Iran War.” No other issue registered at more than 5%.

Amid the focus on economic issues, a plurality of respondents — 42% — said their “personal financial situation” was “the same” as four years earlier. Thirty-six percent said it was “worse” compared with four years earlier, while 22% said it was “better.”

Meanwhile, most respondents (64%) in reliably blue California overwhelmingly said they disapproved of the job President Donald Trump was doing. Another 31% said they approved, and 5% said they weren’t sure.

Asked how much impact they felt the conflict with Iran was having on the U.S. economy, more than two-thirds (67%) of respondents said it was having a “great” deal of impact. Another 16% said it was having “some” impact, while 7% said “not much,” and 8% said “none.”

title: Judge allows Paramount to close $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The deal brings together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+, and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
story: A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
Judge clears way for Paramount to acquire Warner Bros.
The seismic merger will bring together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+, and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
Shortly after the judge’s approval, David Ellison, the CEO and controlling shareholder of Paramount Skydance, announced that Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz would become co-CEO of the combined media giant.
Kreiz will join the company Oct. 5, and the companies said in a statement the deal “is expected to close on October 6.”

“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.

Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.

After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department, the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s Democratic attorney general, Rob Bonta.
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potentially imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.

Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21, which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close ally of President Donald Trump’s. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.

After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News. She has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence.
The merged company pledged to invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called ticking fee kicks in for Paramount Skydance.

In order to build confidence in the merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.

“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
A spokesperson for the California Department of Justice said Wednesday that they are “pleased the court has approved our settlement.”

“Our settlement with Paramount resolves our antitrust concerns in every market we brought in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and centers the needs, concerns, and futures of California workers,” the spokesperson said.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the Block the Merger coalition, urged in an amicus brief that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.

The group criticized the state attorneys general for what it called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld,” the group said.
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.

Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.

title: LSU student says she was raped by a football player who is still on the team
summary: “LSU does really protect their athletes, especially their football players,” says the woman, whose claims are being investigated by the local district attorney.
story: A Louisiana State University student who claims a school football player raped her last year is speaking out about how the school handled her report and the lack of guidance she said she received throughout the process.

Kendall Danielle Francis talked on TikTok about the monthslong Title IX investigation that played out after she reported the October rape to the school. Two days into the current semester, she said, she received an email while she was in class to notify her that the student, who had been suspended for two semesters, had his punishment modified upon appeal to four semesters’ probation. He would remain on campus and could continue to play football, she said.

“Now I am just trying to speak on my story, because LSU does really protect their athletes, especially their football players,” Francis, who was 18 at the time of the alleged incident, said in the Sept. 14 social media post. As a result of the student’s remaining on campus, Francis said, she moved her classes online.
Francis wasn’t aware that filing the Title IX complaint was a separate process from filing criminal charges, a spokesperson for Francis said Wednesday.

“When she filed for Title IX, they [the university] did not tell her she could also contact the police and have them launch a criminal investigation,” a spokesperson said. “She just assumed LSU would do the criminal investigation.”

Francis’ post, however, caught the attention of East Baton Rouge Parish District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose office announced it was launching a criminal investigation. He has requested “all reports, interviews, evidence, and other relevant records” from LSU, the university police and the Baton Rouge Police Department, as well as the coroner’s office, which handles the evidence collection from sexual assault victims.
“This is now an open criminal investigation,” Moore said Sept. 22 in a statement on his agency’s Facebook page.

Francis’ allegations come as accusations that members of a fraternity gang-raped a female Cornell University student for several hours have renewed questions nationwide about whether universities are doing enough to protect students from sexual assault.
LSU President Wade Rousse said in a statement that the university is cooperating with investigators.

“Let me assure everyone that this incident has been handled professionally and that LSU has strictly followed our policies, procedures and best practices, including the Title IX process, to guide our actions to date,” Rousse said.
Title IX is a federal law that requires all universities that receive federal funds to put safeguards in place to protect students from sexual predators.
Francis didn’t respond to several reach-outs from NBC News to discuss her online allegations or share the findings of the Title IX investigation.
In her TikTok video, Francis said she was assaulted at around 4:30 a.m. Oct. 18 “by a football player at LSU.”
“That day basically changed my life,” she said, adding that she “developed pretty severe anxiety” and that after an official diagnosis she began taking medication to manage it.
Francis said that she was taken to the hospital, where she had “a rape kit done,” but that she didn’t initially press charges.
“However, I did go through the Title IX process here at LSU, which took a really, really long time,” she said.

Francis said she returned to school assuming the football player was suspended and under investigation by the police. She said she was in a class when she was notified via email that the alleged attacker was still “accountable” for the rape and would be on probation and allowed to attend classes on campus and play football.

“I was under the impression that because LSU found him responsible that LSU would do their part, that criminal charges, you know, would be pursued,” Francis said in an interview last week with WAFB-TV of Baton Rouge.
For Subscribers

Universities are generally not required to automatically alert the police when a Title IX sexual assault or rape investigation is underway, especially if the survivor requests confidentiality or chooses not to involve law enforcement.
For Subscribers

Francis said in a second TikTok post that she reported the alleged rape this month to LSU police in an attempt to press charges. NBC News has reached out to the agency to confirm that, but so far there has been no response.

The Baton Rouge-based newspaper The Advocate reported that it had obtained the Title IX documents from the case and that they confirm Francis’ assertion that the football player was found responsible for the rape.
Those documents, according to the newspaper, also confirm that his punishment was reduced on appeal from a two-semester suspension to four semesters of probation.

Some of the sexual activity between Francis and the football player was consensual, according to those documents as reported by The Advocate. Still, the football player admitted that he didn’t specifically ask for Francis’ consent before they had intercourse “and did not stop when he later asked and she was silent,” according to the Title IX documents.

Meg Casper Sunstrom, an LSU spokesperson, didn’t confirm the outcome of the Title IX proceedings or the discipline that was handed down to the student. Nor did she respond to questions about whether the football player was at LSU and playing for the team.
“Since there was no criminal complaint filed by the victim, LSU appropriately turned the issue over to our Title IX office as mandated by law,” Sunstrom said in an email.
But she noted that the football player did “self-report” an incident involving his accuser with the LSU Police Department.

Dated Oct. 18, 2025, the report, obtained from LSU via a public records request, said the 19-year-old football player was at the school’s football facility when he called police “due to concerns about potential accusations from the other party.”
The report gave no indication what those potential accusations were.
The incident report says the football player told police that Francis had told him she was mentally unwell and had “thoughts of suicidal ideation.”

The responding officer noted in the report that police had been in touch with Francis four days earlier, on Oct. 14, “regarding a similar incident.” An officer determined that Francis posed no danger to herself and “seemed to be commenting out of spite.”
This time, the report says, when police went to Francis’ on-campus residence, “it was evident that Francis’s mental state was unstable.” The report doesn’t detail the basis for that conclusion.
“She agreed to go to the hospital for further evaluation, and I transported her to Baton Rouge General Hospital for assessment,” the responding officer wrote in his report.
Francis said in her TikTok post that she dreads the possibility of running into her alleged attacker on campus.

“So that made my anxiety really, really bad, because I don’t want to face this person,” she said. “I really just wanted to bring awareness upon this situation, because I’m just dealing with a lot right now, and I think that this story needs to be heard.”

title: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to a low-security correctional facility in southern New Jersey, sources said.
story: Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.

This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison

Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.

Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.

“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”

“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.

He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.

Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”

Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem. Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.

Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof. The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.

Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter.
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.

Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.

Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.

His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July. He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”

title: White House removes CNN from press pool for Trump’s upcoming trip
summary: CNN was previously scheduled to fly on Air Force One and also provide on-the-ground coverage of Trump’s trip.
story: The White House on Wednesday removed CNN from the press pool that’s set to cover a trip by President Donald Trump on Thursday, escalating a feud with the cable network after a federal judge blocked the administration’s push to restrict its media access.

CNN had been designated to travel with Trump on Thursday, according to a press rotation document the White House released Sunday. But when the daily guidance came out for his scheduled visit to a truck manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas, followed by remarks in Durant, Oklahoma, it did not list CNN as providing pool coverage.

The move comes less than a week after a federal judge halted Trump’s effort to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. It also comes after the White House barred CNN from flying on Air Force One over the weekend when Trump traveled to Tennessee, when the network was scheduled to provide pool coverage. (The judge’s order was limited to media access on the White House grounds.)

Emily Kuhn, a spokesperson for CNN, confirmed the cable network’s removal from planned pool coverage but did not provide additional comment. Instead, she pointed to an earlier statement from Theodore Boutrous, an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico in their fight with the White House over press access.

“As we have said from the beginning, the President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process,” Boutrous said in a statement Monday, when the three news outlets asked a federal judge to extend his pause on Trump’s ban.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about CNN’s exclusion from Thursday’s trip.

The White House press pool is a group of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, each day’s designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public.
For Subscribers

The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last week in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
For Subscribers
Other member networks of the pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in pool duties last week in solidarity with CNN.
NBC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the exclusion of CNN for Thursday’s trip and whether it intended to take any action.

Trump has restricted access for other news outlets before. In 2025, he banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and certain events for not referring to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America — his preferred name for the gulf.
The AP sued, and the case continues.

title: LSU student says she was raped by a football player who is still on the team
summary: “LSU does really protect their athletes, especially their football players,” says the woman, whose claims are being investigated by the local district attorney.
story: A Louisiana State University student who claims a school football player raped her last year is speaking out about how the school handled her report and the lack of guidance she said she received throughout the process.

Kendall Danielle Francis talked on TikTok about the monthslong Title IX investigation that played out after she reported the October rape to the school. Two days into the current semester, she said, she received an email while she was in class to notify her that the student, who had been suspended for two semesters, had his punishment modified upon appeal to four semesters’ probation. He would remain on campus and could continue to play football, she said.

“Now I am just trying to speak on my story, because LSU does really protect their athletes, especially their football players,” Francis, who was 18 at the time of the alleged incident, said in the Sept. 14 social media post. As a result of the student’s remaining on campus, Francis said, she moved her classes online.
Francis wasn’t aware that filing the Title IX complaint was a separate process from filing criminal charges, a spokesperson for Francis said Wednesday.

“When she filed for Title IX, they [the university] did not tell her she could also contact the police and have them launch a criminal investigation,” a spokesperson said. “She just assumed LSU would do the criminal investigation.”

Francis’ post, however, caught the attention of East Baton Rouge Parish District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose office announced it was launching a criminal investigation. He has requested “all reports, interviews, evidence, and other relevant records” from LSU, the university police and the Baton Rouge Police Department, as well as the coroner’s office, which handles the evidence collection from sexual assault victims.
“This is now an open criminal investigation,” Moore said Sept. 22 in a statement on his agency’s Facebook page.

Francis’ allegations come as accusations that members of a fraternity gang-raped a female Cornell University student for several hours have renewed questions nationwide about whether universities are doing enough to protect students from sexual assault.
LSU President Wade Rousse said in a statement that the university is cooperating with investigators.

“Let me assure everyone that this incident has been handled professionally and that LSU has strictly followed our policies, procedures and best practices, including the Title IX process, to guide our actions to date,” Rousse said.
Title IX is a federal law that requires all universities that receive federal funds to put safeguards in place to protect students from sexual predators.
Francis didn’t respond to several reach-outs from NBC News to discuss her online allegations or share the findings of the Title IX investigation.
In her TikTok video, Francis said she was assaulted at around 4:30 a.m. Oct. 18 “by a football player at LSU.”
“That day basically changed my life,” she said, adding that she “developed pretty severe anxiety” and that after an official diagnosis she began taking medication to manage it.
Francis said that she was taken to the hospital, where she had “a rape kit done,” but that she didn’t initially press charges.
“However, I did go through the Title IX process here at LSU, which took a really, really long time,” she said.

Francis said she returned to school assuming the football player was suspended and under investigation by the police. She said she was in a class when she was notified via email that the alleged attacker was still “accountable” for the rape and would be on probation and allowed to attend classes on campus and play football.

“I was under the impression that because LSU found him responsible that LSU would do their part, that criminal charges, you know, would be pursued,” Francis said in an interview last week with WAFB-TV of Baton Rouge.
For Subscribers

Universities are generally not required to automatically alert the police when a Title IX sexual assault or rape investigation is underway, especially if the survivor requests confidentiality or chooses not to involve law enforcement.
For Subscribers

Francis said in a second TikTok post that she reported the alleged rape this month to LSU police in an attempt to press charges. NBC News has reached out to the agency to confirm that, but so far there has been no response.

The Baton Rouge-based newspaper The Advocate reported that it had obtained the Title IX documents from the case and that they confirm Francis’ assertion that the football player was found responsible for the rape.
Those documents, according to the newspaper, also confirm that his punishment was reduced on appeal from a two-semester suspension to four semesters of probation.

Some of the sexual activity between Francis and the football player was consensual, according to those documents as reported by The Advocate. Still, the football player admitted that he didn’t specifically ask for Francis’ consent before they had intercourse “and did not stop when he later asked and she was silent,” according to the Title IX documents.

Meg Casper Sunstrom, an LSU spokesperson, didn’t confirm the outcome of the Title IX proceedings or the discipline that was handed down to the student. Nor did she respond to questions about whether the football player was at LSU and playing for the team.
“Since there was no criminal complaint filed by the victim, LSU appropriately turned the issue over to our Title IX office as mandated by law,” Sunstrom said in an email.
But she noted that the football player did “self-report” an incident involving his accuser with the LSU Police Department.

Dated Oct. 18, 2025, the report, obtained from LSU via a public records request, said the 19-year-old football player was at the school’s football facility when he called police “due to concerns about potential accusations from the other party.”
The report gave no indication what those potential accusations were.
The incident report says the football player told police that Francis had told him she was mentally unwell and had “thoughts of suicidal ideation.”

The responding officer noted in the report that police had been in touch with Francis four days earlier, on Oct. 14, “regarding a similar incident.” An officer determined that Francis posed no danger to herself and “seemed to be commenting out of spite.”
This time, the report says, when police went to Francis’ on-campus residence, “it was evident that Francis’s mental state was unstable.” The report doesn’t detail the basis for that conclusion.
“She agreed to go to the hospital for further evaluation, and I transported her to Baton Rouge General Hospital for assessment,” the responding officer wrote in his report.
Francis said in her TikTok post that she dreads the possibility of running into her alleged attacker on campus.

“So that made my anxiety really, really bad, because I don’t want to face this person,” she said. “I really just wanted to bring awareness upon this situation, because I’m just dealing with a lot right now, and I think that this story needs to be heard.”

title: Man accused in plot to attack Texas Capitol building is released on bond
summary: Authorities said he planned to attack the capitol Thursday. He was arrested at his home early Wednesday.
story: The Texas Department of Public Safety confirmed Wednesday that officers foiled a plan to attack the Texas State Capitol in Austin.
According to Texas DPS, officers received credible information about a person planning a violent attack on the Texas State Capitol on Thursday.
Texas DPS said its Criminal Investigations Division special agents worked alongside the FBI to investigate the validity of the threat and the circumstances surrounding the planned attack.
At around 3 a.m. Wednesday, DPS SWAT arrested 40-year-old Benny Caldera Jr. at his residence in Converse, about 15 miles northeast of downtown San Antonio, Texas DPS said.
According to an arrest warrant affidavit, DPS officers spoke to Caldera’s friend, who said he “had made verbal threats to assault the Texas State Capitol Building.”

Caldera’s friend told officers that Caldera said, “I love you, if you don’t see me again,” and explained that, “I am going to the Capitol and I am going to shoot it up,” according to arrest documents.
Arrest documents further state that Caldera told his friend that he was angry at the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and that “these people have to be exterminated.”
For Subscribers
Caldera was transported to the Bexar County Jail and charged with felony terroristic threat against a public servant. He was later released on a $75,000 bond.
For Subscribers
Bexar County court records show that Caldera was previously charged with unlicensed carrying of a weapon in November 2023.
According to Texas DPS, leadership notified legislators of the threat and arrest Wednesday, and the Capitol remains open for regular operating hours.
Texas DPS said officers will continue to have an increased presence at the Texas Capitol to protect employees, visitors and state officials.

title: A California showdown with national implications: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, we take a look at where the billionaire tax campaign in California stands and what it signals about the Democratic Party’s direction.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we take a look at where the billionaire tax campaign in California stands and what it signals about the Democratic Party’s direction. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines President Donald Trump’s efforts to reassure a skeptical public on AI.
— Adam Wollner
A California showdown with national implications

California Democrats avoided what would have been a brutal and costly intraparty fight for governor when progressive activist Tom Steyer finished third in the all-party primary this summer, leaving former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra as the clear favorite in a one-on-one November matchup against Republican Steve Hilton.
But there’s a battle brewing further down the ballot that could have even broader implications for the party, both in the state and nationally.

Voters in California will decide this fall whether to implement a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires. Listed as “Proposition 40,” the ballot measure is shaping up as one of the most expensive campaigns in the country this year, with roughly $100 million already spent or booked on ads through Election Day, according to AdImpact. Tech leaders in Silicon Valley, most notably Google co-founder Sergey Brin, have aggressively lined up against the billionaire tax, which was pushed by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West.

As we’ve reported, the proposal emerged as a major fault line for Democrats in the state’s race for governor and in the not-so-invisible 2028 presidential primary. Becerra and term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom are against it, while Steyer and Rep. Ro Khanna are for it.

Meanwhile, a slew of other prominent California Democrats — including former Vice President Kamala Harris, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla — have not taken firm public stances on the ballot measure.

A new poll out today underscores why the party is scattered on the issue. According to an NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group survey, 48% of likely California voters back the billionaire tax, while 38% oppose it and 14% are undecided. While it’s certainly a more promising result for proponents of the measure than opponents, it still falls short of majority support.

Among Democrats, however, 67% said they will vote for the proposal and 19% said they will vote against it. One of the arguments from the anti-billionaire-tax side is that wealthy Californians will flee the state. The poll showed that 59% of respondents said they were not concerned about that potential outcome, compared with 41% who said they were concerned.

Passage of a first-of-its-kind billionaire tax would be a major shot in the arm for progressives heading into the 2028 campaign. While deep-blue California is not necessarily representative of the entire nation, a victory would further highlight the populist streak running through the party’s base and the electorate at large. A national NBC News poll earlier this month asked registered voters whether 15 different attributes would make them more or less likely to support a candidate. The most popular? Raising taxes on billionaires.

That’s the sort of energy potential White House contenders like Khanna are hoping to tap into: He’s set to team up with Sen. Bernie Sanders for rallies in San Francisco and Los Angeles in the coming days in support of the wealth tax.
Trump has a new name for AI — but not regulations
The world’s tech leaders — 21 men and one woman — were out in full force for a White House lunch with President Donald Trump Tuesday.
Their cumulative wealth? Hard to estimate. Their promise to voluntarily regulate artificial intelligence? Perhaps equally so.

To try to reassure a skittish public about the safety of the biggest technological transformation since the internet, Trump, a master of rebranding, signed an executive order requiring all federal agencies to rename AI as “superintelligence,” or “SI.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

With considerable fanfare, the White House heralded a new accord to develop internal safety controls to prevent rogue agents from spinning out of control. The self-policing agreement includes risk reviews and auditing by third parties. Trump called the voluntary agreement “morally binding.” Tech journalist Kara Swisher called it a “pinky promise.”

Ironically, the White House position against any regulation came on the same day Anthropic submitted its security filing for its long-awaited IPO. It devoted almost one-third of the filing to warning investors the technology may pose “existential risks to humanity,” including that advanced AI models could manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other unpredictable behaviors.

Last April, Anthropic held back its Mythos model citing potential dangers. In July, OpenAI models hacked the Hugging Face AI startup. In September, leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind called for slowing down advanced models because of safety concerns. And last week, OpenAI revealed its tools had hacked dozens of sites, including governments, and scrapped plans to release its newest model next month.

In an interview with “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told Kristen Welker, “AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths,” adding, “There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools.” Asked about voluntary regulation, he said, “No one thinks self-regulation is enough.”

In response to growing political concerns in both parties, Trump said yesterday, “I will never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.” During a White House summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two rivals in the AI race issued a vague agreement to communicate about threats.

At the White House yesterday, competition over AI was top of mind over cooperation. Trump told the tech CEOs, “You’re going to have a winner, or you’re going to have a loser,” adding, “We’re leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way.” That same day, Senate Democrats tried to pass legislation to regulate AI by unanimous consent, but Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, objected.

The debate has even caught the attention of the pope. Speaking to reporters yesterday, Pope Leo questioned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s commitment to safety. Huang, who has called for a hands-off approach on regulation, was among the guests at the state dinner for Xi and yesterday’s White House meeting.

“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the pope said of Huang. He added, “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
